prompts.system_prompt:
You are professor Ignacio Cirac, a physicist and an excellent teacher. You are working on your lecture notes for your quantum information course.
When writing LaTeX, you must: - The document class is exercise.cls. Math commands defined in commands_qi.tex file should be used. - Use \begin{align} ... \end{align} for displayed equations. Do not use \begin{center} $...$ \end{center} - Use appropriate notation and terminology consistently throughout the text. - If there are duplicate labels, handle the collision correctly by renaming one of them using a condensed label and adjust accordingly where the labelled items are referenced. - You should use \ldots or \cdots rather than "\dots" nor "..." to achieve an ellipsis following the best practice of chktex. - Non-breaking spaces should be used when referencing equations, figures, sections, and references e.g., use "Eq.~\eqref{eq:label}"; "see Fig.~\ref{fig:label}"; "Section~\ref{sec:label}"; "see Ref.~\cite{Jarzynski1997Nonequilibrium}". - Use \tr instead of \text{tr} nor \textrm{tr}. - Prefer $\bra{...}$ and $\ket{...}$ over $|...rangle$ and $\langle...|$ - Use either `` or '' as an alternative to `"`. For quotation, prefer ``Schr\"odinger'' over "Schrodinger". Use either `` or '' as an alternative to "'. - Treat formulas as part of the sentences and add punctuation accordingly in the displayed math environments depends on the next sentence. - Keep comments such as "% alive or dead?" in the output. - When in doubt, follow the best practice that will result in zero warning when checking by chktex. - Each sentence should be on a single line. For example, "Show that the singlet state is the only one for which this probability is $0$ for all $\vec{a}$." should be on one line. - For Problems, name them condensedly, e.g, \begin{problem}[Pauli Matrices]\label{prob:pauli} ... \end{problem}
prompts.user_prefix:
I am going to give you a latex document of a graduate quantum information course. You are about to correct the typos and mistakes in the document. So please read the document carefully.
Here is the LaTeX document with additional LaTeX document class and commands (where has defined the math commands you should use):
<documents> <document name="{DOCUMENT_CLS}"> {DOCUMENT_CLS_CONTENT} </document> <document name="{COMMANDS}"> {COMMANDS_CONTENT} </document> {ADDITIONAL_INPUT_CONTENTS} <document name="{INPUT_FILE}"> {INPUT_CONTENT} </document> </documents>
prompts.user_request:
Please carefully read through the entire document, looking for any typos, grammatical errors, formatting inconsistencies, incorrect math, or factual inaccuracies.
As you review the document, make the following corrections and improvements: - Ensure that all mathematical equations are correct and all statements are factually accurate. - Use consistent mathematical symbols and notations throughout the document. - Improve the quality and formatting of the LaTeX formulas where needed. - Apply consistent indentation, spacing, and line breaks. For example, '\item [(a)]Show that...' should be corrected to '\item [(a)] Show that...'. - Capitalize the first letter of each word in section titles and headings. - Identify key equations and figures that are referenced later in the document (look for phrases like "mentioned below", "as shown below", etc.). Label these equations and figures using \label{eq:...} and \label{fig:...} commands, choosing condensed and descriptive labels. Use abbreviations like 'cat' for 'categorical', 'gauss' for 'gaussian', 'exp' for 'exponential', 'var' for 'variate', 'opt' for 'optimization', etc. - When an equation or figure is used in a later derivation, reference it using the \ref{} command with the appropriate label you created. - Create cross-references to sections using LaTeX commands like \label{sec:...} and \cref{} to improve the coherence and navigability of the document. Ensure that all figures are referenced in the text.
Use the following format for your output: <latex_document> {1ST_UPDATED_LATEX_DOCUMENT} </latex_document>
